evidence.excerpt: This paper presents a structured cost-of-quality (CoQ) data collection exercise conducted at a contract electronics manufacturer in Vojvodina producing between 40 and 200 units per batch across roughly 120 active product variants. Using a modified PAF (prevention–appraisal–failure) framework, the study captured 14 months of expenditure records and reclassified 23 cost categories previously buried in overhead accounts. Prevention costs accounted for 18% of total quality costs, appraisal for 41%, and internal failure for the remaining 41%, with external failure costs near zero due to strict outgoing inspection. Regression analysis on monthly data showed a statistically significant negative relationship between appraisal spending and internal failure costs (R² = 0.61), but only above a threshold appraisal intensity of roughly 2.3% of turnover. Below that threshold, increased inspection had no measurable effect on defect escape rates. The findings suggest that the company's inspection resources were concentrated at final test while upstream in-circuit test capacity was insufficient. Recommendations for rebalancing inspection effort are provided, along with a simple spreadsheet model validated against the 14-month dataset.
